content: Ethanol, when consumed in sublethal doses, exerts psychoactive effects. For detailed information, refer to the specific effects of alcohol on the body by dose. Due to its ability to alter human consciousness, ethanol is classified as a drug. Blood alcohol concentrations (BAC) of 0.4% to 0.5% or higher are commonly fatal. In the United States, approximately half of all fatalities in car accidents are associated with alcohol-related crashes. There is no completely safe level of alcohol consumption for driving, as the risk of a fatal car accident increases exponentially with the driver’s blood alcohol level. Ethanol interacts harmfully with several other drugs, including barbiturates, benzodiazepines, narcotics, and phenothiazines. These interactions can amplify the adverse effects of both ethanol and the other substances. Within the human body, ethanol is metabolized into acetaldehyde by the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase, and subsequently into acetic acid by acetaldehyde dehydrogenase. Acetaldehyde, the intermediate product of this metabolic process, is more toxic than ethanol itself and is implicated in most of the clinical effects of alcohol. Acetaldehyde has been shown to increase the risk of developing liver cirrhosis, various forms of cancer, and alcoholism. Some individuals possess less effective forms of one or both of these enzymes, leading to more severe symptoms from ethanol consumption compared to others. Conversely, individuals with acquired ethanol tolerance have higher levels of these enzymes, allowing them to metabolize ethanol more rapidly. The amount of ethanol in the body is typically measured by blood alcohol content (BAC), which is expressed as milligrams of ethanol per 100 milliliters of blood. Small doses of ethanol generally induce euphoria and relaxation, often making individuals more talkative and less inhibited, though they may also exhibit poor judgment. At higher doses (BAC > 100 mg/dL), ethanol acts as a central nervous system depressant, leading to progressively severe effects such as impaired sensory and motor function, slowed cognition, stupor, unconsciousness, and potentially death. Chronic consumption of alcoholic beverages has been identified as a significant contributing factor to elevated blood triglyceride levels, which are associated with various health risks.
